clue.text: See 5 down
Desperate as a docked donkey

indicators.note: a docked tail is cut short, so the word after it loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written
moke is British slang for a donkey

explanation.surface: A donkey with its tail cut off is in a frantic, desperate state.
explanation.walkthrough: Moke is old British slang for a donkey; dock its tail and MOK follows A to give AMOK.
explanation.definitionFit: Running amok means behaving wildly and frantically, out of control like someone driven to desperation.

clue.text: Vicar, say, enjoys living on immoral earnings, say

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the preceding phrase and take the word it sounds like

parts.note: earnings are income, and bent means crooked or immoral

explanation.surface: A clergyman is scandalously supported by a pimp's income.
explanation.walkthrough: A parish benefice is called a living, and a vicar holding one is said to enjoy it, so the link words are themselves churchy; the phrase spoken aloud gives INCUMBENT.
explanation.definitionFit: The incumbent of a parish is the clergyman currently holding its benefice, and a vicar is one example.

clue.text: Periodical too wise, we hear, to admit a nobleman

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece is placed inside the other
we hear says the phrase before it is taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: spoken, too wise sounds like two Ys, the letter Y twice
an earl is a British noble

explanation.surface: A magazine too clever for its own good lets an aristocrat in.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter Y is spelt out wye, so too wise is heard as two Ys; they surround EARL to make Y-EARL-Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Periodical as an adjective means recurring at intervals, and yearly is one such interval.

clue.text: Clumsy splices start with slices

parts.note: to start is to jump in surprise
slices are cuts

explanation.surface: An unskilled film editor begins joining footage by hacking it into slices.
explanation.definitionFit: A jump cut is an abrupt film edit that breaks continuity, a crude join between two shots.

clue.text: Sibling joy: the takeaway fry-up with Ma, Pa and, perhaps, the 10s or the 26s

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters could be arranged some other way
a takeaway suggests something being removed from the next phrase

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, before a letter goes
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A family enjoys a takeaway breakfast together, like the cheerful households on television.
explanation.walkthrough: The R is taken out of fry-up, then all the letters are rearranged. The 10s are the Larkins of The Darling Buds of May; the 26s are the Waltons of the American TV series.
explanation.definitionFit: Both television families are idealised examples of a close, contented household living together harmoniously.

clue.text: Unblended Scotch left in family oven

parts.note: single malt whisky is not blended

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: kin are family
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone stashes their single-malt whisky in a relative's oven.
explanation.walkthrough: Unblended Scotch is single malt, as opposed to blended whisky; the left goes inside the family word rather than after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A malt kiln is the heated chamber in which germinated barley is dried, a kind of oven.

clue.text: Primitive cry going out for a takeaway

indicators.note: going out means going round the outside of another piece

parts.note: taken as written
Ur- is a prefix meaning primitive or original

explanation.surface: A caveman's grunt heard as someone heads off to buy dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur- as in Ur-text or Urheimat is the prefix for the earliest, original form of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Curry is a staple of British takeaway food, an example of a meal bought ready to eat.

clue.text: Bog standard TV drama? I wash my hands of it!

definitions.text: I wash my hands of it!

parts.note: bog is British slang for a lavatory; standard is just surface padding in the phrase bog standard
a soap opera is a serial television drama

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a mediocre television drama in disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: Bog standard is British for utterly ordinary; I wash my hands of it usually means disowning something, but here it is literally what one does with the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Toilet soap is the mild soap used for washing hands and body, so one literally washes hands with it.

clue.text: Could be Sixth Form to politically correct young woman

parts.note: taken as written
PC is the usual abbreviation
a lass is a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl moves up to the sixth form, all very right-on.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sixth Form is the final year group in a British secondary school, for students aged 16 to 18.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sixth Form is the highest year group in a British school, an example of an elite or senior class.

clue.text: God of home, family and Hull's library?

parts.note: a lar is a Roman household god
kin are family

explanation.surface: A list of what a household holds sacred, ending with a city's book collection.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet Philip Larkin was librarian at the University of Hull for thirty years; the question mark flags the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet ran Hull University's library for decades, so his name stands for that institution by association.

clue.text: Silent monkey milked silent cows here!

indicators.note: milked means worked and squeezed, so the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An absurd farmyard where a mute monkey milks mute cows.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton Keynes is an English new town famous for its concrete cow sculptures, which are certainly silent.
explanation.definitionFit: The town's famous Concrete Cows sculptures are a well-known landmark, so silent cows locate the place.

clue.text: This conception turned out well

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the ... Conception of Christian doctrine
second meaning: perfectly dressed and groomed

explanation.walkthrough: Turned out well reads as a successful result, but it means well turned out, flawlessly presented.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective names the Catholic doctrine of Mary's sinless conception and also describes spotless, impeccable grooming.

clue.text: Back English measures to score a duck

indicators.note: back means the pieces are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
ems are printers' measures of type width

explanation.surface: A cricket fan backs England's tactics to get a batsman out for nought.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck in cricket is a score of zero, which is the false trail; here it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Smee is an old dialect name for a wild duck such as the smew or wigeon.

clue.text: So Antony of Brutus finally might lie with gusto

indicators.note: might suggests the words could be otherwise, a possible rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mark Antony speaks of Brutus with insincere relish, as in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar.
explanation.walkthrough: Antony's funeral speech for Caesar is ironic, but at the play's end he sincerely praises Brutus as the noblest Roman of them all.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who delivers praise of a dead person is one, as Antony does over Brutus's body.

clue.text: China's Long March?

parts.note: surface reading: Mao's famous retreat of the Red Army in 1934-35
setter's reading: a march is a border, so a lengthy frontier barrier in China

explanation.walkthrough: March here is the old word for a border region, as in the Welsh Marches.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient fortification ran thousands of miles along China's northern frontier, a very lengthy boundary.

clue.text: Singers of the lost generation

parts.note: surface reading: vocalists from the era after the First World War
setter's reading: male singers who lost the power to father children

explanation.walkthrough: The Lost Generation usually means those who came of age in the First World War; here generation means procreation.
explanation.definitionFit: These were male sopranos castrated in boyhood to preserve a high voice, so unable to reproduce.

clue.text: Lost memory? One might have a beef here

parts.note: something past is gone, lost
RAM is computer memory
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone whose computer has crashed and wiped its memory has a grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: A beef is slang for a complaint, which the surface invites; the definition is the meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastrami is a seasoned smoked cured beef, so it counts as a type of beef product.

clue.text: Dutch Redcoat on board

parts.note: surface reading: a Dutch-born British soldier aboard ship
setter's reading: something from Holland in a red wax rind served on a cheeseboard

explanation.walkthrough: Redcoat was the nickname for a British soldier; board here is a cheeseboard, not a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: This Dutch cheese is sold in a distinctive red wax coating and appears on cheeseboards.

clue.text: Concede old ledge added now

parts.note: surface reading: admit to an old point
setter's reading: add the word ledge and you have today's form of the word

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an archaic verb; append ledge and it becomes the modern word for concede.
explanation.definitionFit: This obsolete verb meant to admit or recognise, the older form of today's acknowledge.

clue.text: Get Tom's goat? That's the last thing one would do!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: annoy a tomcat, to put out being to irritate

definitions.text: That's the last thing one would do!
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the nightly chore before going to bed

explanation.walkthrough: The last thing one would do usually means something one would never do; here it is literally the final task at bedtime.
explanation.definitionFit: To be put out is to be annoyed, as is a cat with its goat got; letting the cat out is traditionally done just before bed.

clue.text: The other sideboard

parts.note: surface reading: a second piece of dining-room furniture
setter's reading: split it as side and board, a board for messages from the other side, the afterlife

explanation.walkthrough: Split sideboard into side and board: the other side is the afterlife, reached by a spiritualist's lettered board.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiritualists use this lettered board with a pointer to receive messages supposedly from the dead.

clue.text: Car ferry's repeated verbal instructions to the galley

indicators.note: verbal instructions are spoken ones, so we take the sound of the words

parts.words: repeated verbal instructions to the galley
parts.note: oarsmen in a galley are told to row, said twice

explanation.surface: A ferry captain keeps shouting orders down to the ship's kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: The galley seems to be a ship's kitchen; it is the old oared warship.
explanation.definitionFit: Ro-ro stands for roll-on roll-off, the design of ferry that vehicles drive straight on and off.

clue.text: A knight, a wife, a dam

parts.note: K is the chess notation for king, but N or K is used for knight; here K for knight
taken as written
Eve was made from Adam's rib, so rib is a jocular word for a wife
taken as written

explanation.surface: A list like a medieval tale's cast: a knight, his lady and a barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: K is the abbreviation for knight in honours such as KBE. Kariba is the great hydroelectric dam on the Zambezi between Zambia and Zimbabwe.
explanation.definitionFit: Kariba is the name of a major dam on the Zambezi river in southern Africa.

clue.text: Hawks often here with swan; not a good combination

parts.note: a pen is a female swan

indicators.note: a combination mixes things together, so these letters are combined in a new order

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Birds of prey and a swan make a poor mix.
explanation.walkthrough: Hawks seem to be birds; they are hard-line military strategists in Washington.
explanation.definitionFit: The US Department of Defense headquarters is where military hawks, advocates of aggressive policy, typically work.

clue.text: Truth in failing variety clubs

indicators.note: failing means collapsing, so these letters fall into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games

explanation.surface: Honest talk about the decline of variety theatre and music-hall clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: Variety clubs suggest music-hall entertainment venues, but clubs is the card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Veracity is conformity to facts, accuracy and honesty, a close synonym for truth.

clue.text: This angler knew the score

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Izaak ..., author of The Compleat Angler
second meaning: Sir William ..., the composer, who wrote scores

explanation.walkthrough: Knew the score usually means understood the situation; here a score is written music, which one composer knew well.
explanation.definitionFit: Two famous Englishmen share the surname: one wrote the classic fishing book, the other was a twentieth-century composer.
